AccountDeleteRequest.description:
Explicit confirmation, so a stray click cannot destroy an account.

``confirm`` is declared **optional** even though the request is refused
without it, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight.

Making it required would let the enforced schema reject an absent value with
422 while the handler rejects a wrong value with 400 -- two refusal paths to
the same decision, on the one operation in the API that cannot be undone.
A safety interlock on an irreversible action wants exactly one path, owned by
the code that performs the action, so that it cannot be relaxed by a change
to a schema. Leaving it optional here means every non-``"DELETE"`` value --
absent, empty, misspelled, wrong type -- takes the same branch and gets the
same actionable message.

The field is still documented, so a generated client still knows to send it.
AccountDeleteRequest.title: AccountDeleteRequest

AccountDeleteResponse.description:
Result of a tombstone deletion.

``r2_delete_failures`` is deliberately part of the success body rather than
being swallowed: reporting "deleted" while a resume object is still live in
object storage would be a false claim (D-07).

r2_delete_failures.description: Object keys that could not be removed from R2. Empty is the happy path.
r2_delete_failures.title: R2 Delete Failures

AccountDeleteResponse.title: AccountDeleteResponse

either way. It stays typed as an open object because the keys that have not
been promoted to columns yet still vary per user.

assessment_answers.description: The subject's own answers. Keyed by intent rather than after the table they come from, so an internal schema name does not become part of a public contract.
assessment_answers.title: Assessment Answers

profile.description: The profile document. Assembled from the profile tables since Phase 2a; open-ended because the unpromoted keys genuinely vary per user.
profile.title: Profile

AccountExportResponse.title: AccountExportResponse

The server prepends its own system message carrying RAG context assembled
from the profile, the company network, and the user's resume text -- so a
client must not send a system message of its own expecting it to be
honoured.

``GET /assessments`` -- the five instruments and where the caller stands.

The person-side items, ordered for this respondent.

The payload carries ``blocks``, not ``dimensions``. The client renders it
verbatim: it must not sort, group, re-shuffle, or reorder options. Ordering
is server-authoritative because two independent PRNGs in two languages
diverging is silent, and a divergence corrupts a resumed session's ordering
rather than raising (D-04).

AssessmentScoringJobStatus.description:
Documentation-only union of the three poll responses.

Which member comes back is determined by ``{kind}`` in the path, not by
anything in the body -- the same reason ``AssessmentSubmissionResponse``
cannot be an OpenAPI discriminated union.  Do not validate against this;
validate against :data:`SCORING_JOB_RESPONSES`.
AssessmentScoringJobStatus.title: AssessmentScoringJobStatus

AssessmentSubmissionRequest.description:
Documentation-only union of the five submission bodies.

Do not validate against this. Union members here are open models, so
pydantic's smart matching will accept almost anything into the first one
that fits -- which is precisely why the route enforces
:data:`SUBMISSION_REQUESTS` per kind rather than this.
AssessmentSubmissionRequest.title: AssessmentSubmissionRequest

AssessmentSubmissionResponse.description:
Documentation-only union of the five submission results.

Which member comes back is determined by ``{kind}`` in the path, not by
anything in the body, so this cannot be an OpenAPI discriminated union --
3.1 keys a discriminator off a property of the payload, and the
discriminator here is the URL. The union is the honest encoding of "one of
these five, and the path tells you which".

AssessmentSubmitResponse.description:
Deliberately does not carry the six dimension scores.

The documented threat to this instrument is aspirational answering by a user
self-profiling for matching. Handing back the six numbers gives a retaking
respondent a gradient to optimise against -- it teaches the
item-to-dimension mapping that the shuffle and the interleave exist to hide.
AssessmentSubmitResponse.title: AssessmentSubmitResponse

CompanyDetailResponse.description:
One company's full stored research profile.

``id`` is the integer primary key and appears in the URL, so this endpoint
enumerates: an authenticated caller can walk the ids and read the whole
network. Part 4.2 replaces it with a UUID ``public_id``.

``profile`` is the serialised ``CompanyProfile`` from

One company in the list.

Deliberately not the full profile: the list ships the fields a card renders
and ``GET /companies/{id}`` ships the rest. The endpoint this pattern
replaces had no list at all, so every screen that wanted several companies
fetched the whole research document for each.

CultureMatchEntry.description:
One scored company.

``top_matching_dimensions`` and ``top_mismatching_dimensions`` are the two
highest- and two lowest-scoring dimensions, and ``fit_summary`` is the
sentence built from them.
CultureMatchEntry.title: CultureMatchEntry

Job-seeker dashboard summary.

``recentActivity`` and ``recommendations`` are static placeholders in the

Landing-page interest form.

IdentityResponse.description:
``GET /me`` -- who the caller is, and nothing else.

Four columns off ``users``. No ``profileData``: shipping the whole user
document to render a nav bar is the god-endpoint problem, and the client
that wants the profile asks for the profile.
IdentityResponse.title: IdentityResponse

IdentityUpdateRequest.description:
``PATCH /me``.

``name`` is the only writable identity field, and the omissions are
deliberate rather than pending. Changing ``email`` has to re-run
verification or it is an account-takeover primitive; ``role`` is a privilege
boundary and is not something an account may grant itself.

IntakeClaimLinkRequest.description:
``mode: "link"`` -- file a submission while already signed in.

Same body as a submission minus the email, which comes from the JWT.
Recording the body's email instead would let a signed-in user file a
submission under someone else's address.

IntakeClaimRegisterRequest.description:
``mode: "register"`` -- create a new account from a finished submission.

The account's email comes from the submission, never from this body: the
submitter proved control of it by receiving nothing, but they did type it
into a form that is already recorded, and letting the claim body override it
would turn a guessed submission id into an account under any address.
IntakeClaimRegisterRequest.title: IntakeClaimRegisterRequest

IntakeClaimRequest.description:
Documentation-only union of the four claim bodies.

Do not validate against this; the route enforces :data:`CLAIM_REQUESTS` per
mode. Unlike the assessment union, this one *is* discriminated on a property
of the payload, so a generated client can narrow it.
IntakeClaimRequest.title: IntakeClaimRequest

IntakeClaimResponse.description:
Documentation-only union of the four claim results.

``register`` answers 201 and the rest answer 200, and the bodies differ:
two carry a session (a JWT cookie plus a CSRF token), one carries the
quiz-completion flag, one is a bare acknowledgement. Unifying the request
did not unify these, for the same reason it did not unify the five
assessment results.
IntakeClaimResponse.title: IntakeClaimResponse

IntakeClaimSessionRequest.description:
``mode: "session"`` -- adopt an anonymous Work Pulse Lite-Lite session.

The one mode with no submission behind it. Called right after login when
``sessionStorage`` still holds answers from the ``/start`` flow.
IntakeClaimSessionRequest.title: IntakeClaimSessionRequest

IntakeClaimSignInRequest.description:
``mode: "sign_in"`` -- attach a submission to an existing account.

The email must match the one on the submission, so a submission cannot be
attached to an unrelated account by guessing its id.
IntakeClaimSignInRequest.title: IntakeClaimSignInRequest

Step 2 of 2. The server HEADs the object before recording the row.

a submission pointing at a key that holds nothing.

Step 1 of 2. The browser PUTs the file to ``upload_url``.

``submission_id`` is a v4 UUID and is the only thing protecting an anonymous
submission -- there is no account to authorise against, so the object key is
deliberately unguessable.

LegacyError.description:
The pre-Phase-1 error body: ``{"error": "..."}``.

Handlers return this from their own explicit failure branches, and Phase 1a
keeps every one of them byte-for-byte.  It coexists with
:class:`ProblemDetailResponse`, which is what the Phase 0 error handlers
produce for anything a handler did not catch itself.

The two shapes are why ``src/shared/api/apiError.ts`` reads both.  Phase 1b
collapses them by moving handlers onto ``solverah.errors.ApiError``.
LegacyError.title: LegacyError

LoginResponse.description:
Successful login. The JWT arrives as an HttpOnly cookie, not in the body.

``csrfToken`` is the double-submit half of the scheme: the client stores it
in memory and echoes it as ``X-CSRF-TOKEN`` on every state-changing request.
Appendix B calls this scheme correct and preserved verbatim.
LoginResponse.title: LoginResponse

LogoutResponse.description:
Always ``{"message": "logout successful"}``.

The cookie is cleared with ``Set-Cookie`` on this response.  Note that the
JWT itself remains valid until it expires -- clearing the cookie ends the
browser session but cannot revoke the token, which is exactly what Part 5.3's
database-backed refresh tokens are for.
LogoutResponse.title: LogoutResponse

ManagerMatchResult.description: Deterministic scoring merged with the LLM-generated narrative.

order.title: Order

A page of scored companies.

``total_companies_scored`` is carried alongside the page because it is what
the UI puts in "N companies scored", and a client cannot derive it from a
page. It is also the honest measure of P0-2: it counts the rows this request
pulled into Python and scored, every time, with no index and no cache.

Passwordless sign-in result.

Same envelope as :class:`LoginResponse` but with the summary user: this path
does not return ``profileData`` or the assessment-completion flags, and the
difference is preserved rather than harmonised.
PasswordResetVerifyResponse.title: PasswordResetVerifyResponse

PathPreferencesDocument.description:
``GET|PUT /me/path-preferences`` -- the three career-search preferences.

The endpoint this replaces was write-only and answered ``{"message": ...}``,
so a client had no way to read back what it had saved and had to keep its
own copy or dig the values out of the profile blob. A resource that can be
read is most of what the redesign is for.

Null on every field means the user has not set them. The fields are optional
on the *response* and required on :class:`PathPreferencesPutRequest`,
because "not yet answered" is a real state and "answered with nothing" is
not -- the scorer branches on all three.
PathPreferencesDocument.title: PathPreferencesDocument

PathPreferencesPutRequest.description:
``PUT /me/path-preferences``.

PUT rather than POST: all three fields are written together and the write
replaces whatever was there, so the verb matches what happens. Each is
validated against a closed set server-side -- the path scorer branches on
them, and an unrecognised value would silently change ranking rather than
fail.

PathSuggestionJobStatus.description:
``GET /me/path-suggestion-jobs/{job_id}``.

On ``succeeded``, ``result`` is byte-for-byte what ``GET
/me/path-suggestions`` would have returned -- the job runs the same service
function -- so a client's rendering logic does not fork between the two
paths.

The job also warms ``path_cache`` on the way through, which means the
synchronous GET is a cache hit immediately after a job succeeds. A client
mid-migration can therefore poll the job and then read the old endpoint,
and neither call pays for the scoring twice.

Scored and narrated career paths, cached per user.

A 400 with ``career_status_not_set`` means the profile is missing a field
the scorer requires, and the client should prompt for it. A 500 means O*NET
or the narrator failed, and the client should retry.
PathSuggestionsResponse.title: PathSuggestionsResponse

ProblemDetailError.description: One field-level entry inside a problem document's ``errors`` array.

ProblemDetailResponse.description:
RFC 9457 problem document, as emitted by ``solverah.errors``.

Served with ``Content-Type: application/problem+json``.  This is the body
for anything the handler did not answer itself: an unhandled exception, a
404 on an unknown path, a 405, a 413 over ``MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH``, a 429 from
the limiter.

ProfileDocument.description:
``GET|PATCH /me/profile`` -- the profile half, in an envelope.

The envelope is the point. Returning the document bare would leave nowhere
to put a ``version`` and no way to add one later without colliding with a
profile key of the same name.

P0-1 is fixed as of Phase 2a and ``version`` is *not* here yet, which is
deliberate: the fix is server-side compare-and-swap on ``profiles.version``,
and it needs no cooperation from the client. Exposing the version becomes
worth doing when a client wants to say "write this only if you still have
what I read" -- an If-Match, not a field.

profile.description: The profile document. Assembled from the profile tables since Phase 2a; open-ended because the unpromoted keys genuinely vary per user.

ProfilePatchRequest.description:
``PATCH /me/profile``.

Merged over the stored document rather than replacing it, and filtered by
``validators.clean_profile_data`` first -- an unrecognised key is dropped,
not rejected, which is why the inner object stays open.

profile.description: Partial profile. Merged over the stored document; unknown keys are stripped.
profile.title: Profile

Quizzes to generate insights for.

wired up. It is paginated anyway, and that is the point of doing it now --

``/complete``; 3c deleted that route once the frontend had moved, so this

``status`` is one of ``queued``, ``running``, ``succeeded``, ``failed``; the

SessionFlags.description:
Per-user booleans the shell needs before it can decide what to render.

They live in their own object rather than at the top level so a flag can be
added without the client having to distinguish "new flag" from "new identity
field", and so the whole set can be cached under one key.
SessionFlags.title: SessionFlags

SessionResponse.description:
``GET /auth/session`` -- the cheap session probe, and the fix for P0-3.

The endpoint it replaces on the app-boot path is ``GET /profile``, which
returned the entire user document *and* wrote an ``AuditLog`` row on every
read.  Session restore fires on every page load, so the highest-volume table
in the system was written synchronously on the hottest endpoint and a
request that ought to be servable from a read replica took a write lock.

This returns identity, the CSRF token, and the flags -- no ``profileData``,
no audit row, no commit.  A client that wants the profile asks
``GET /me/profile`` for it, which is the whole point of the split.
SessionResponse.title: SessionResponse

SessionUser.description:
The user object returned on a successful login.

``profileData`` is the entire profile document.  Shipping the whole user
document on every session restore is the god-endpoint problem Part 5.2
splits apart; it is documented here rather than quietly trimmed, because
trimming it would break the frontend that reads it.

Phase 2a changed where it comes from -- six tables rather than one JSON
column -- and changed nothing about what it contains, which is why this
model did not move.

profileData.description: The profile document. Assembled from the profile tables since Phase 2a; open-ended because the unpromoted keys genuinely vary per user.
profileData.title: Profiledata

SessionUser.title: SessionUser

accessTokenCookie.description: HttpOnly JWT set by POST /api/v1/login. Not readable by JavaScript, so it is paired with the CSRF header below on every state-changing method.
accessTokenCookie.name: access_token_cookie

csrfHeader.description: Value of the csrf_access_token cookie, echoed by the client. Required on POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.
csrfHeader.name: X-CSRF-TOKEN

info.description:
PUT /me/skills - write the full set of proficiency ratings.

PUT rather than the PATCH this replaces, because the write is a wholesale
replacement of the ratings map, not a merge into it. Also sets
skills_proficiency_confirmed so the rating modal stops re-prompting.
info.title: Solverah API

post.description: Responds with `text/event-stream`, not JSON: one `data: {"chunk": ...}` frame per token, then `data: {"done": true, "model": ...}`. A failure that happens mid-stream is delivered as a `data: {"error": ...}` frame on a 200, because the status line has already been sent.
post.summary: Stream a chat turn from the AI agent

get.description:
GET /assessments - the five instruments and where this user stands.

New in Phase 1b. Without it a client has to hard-code the five kind keys and
work out completion from three unrelated places: user_intake timestamps, two
profile_data keys, and the person-side tables.
get.summary: List the assessment catalogue with this user's completion state

get.description:
GET /assessments/{kind}/form - the items, ordered for this respondent.

Only `core` serves a form; the other four are rendered from definitions the
client ships with, and asking for theirs is a 404 rather than an empty
payload that implies one might arrive.

The payload carries `blocks`, not `dimensions`. The client renders it
verbatim: it must not sort, group, re-shuffle, or reorder options. Ordering
is server-authoritative because two independent PRNGs in two languages
diverging is silent, and a divergence corrupts a resumed session's ordering
rather than raising (D-04).
get.summary: Fetch an assessment's items, ordered for this respondent

post.description:
The only way the provider-scored instruments score since Phase 3c. Takes the body `POST /assessments/{kind}/submissions` used to take for these kinds; answers `202` with a job handle instead of blocking on the provider. Poll `GET /assessments/{kind}/scoring-jobs/{job_id}` until `status` is `succeeded` or `failed`.

Only the three provider-scored instruments have this operation: `work_pulse`, `wpll`, `manager_match`. `core` and `focus_type` score deterministically in-process and answer `404` here -- they are served by the synchronous submit route, which since Phase 3c serves only them.

**This shares one rate-limit budget with the synchronous submit for the same instrument.** The limit bounds provider spend, and spend does not move when the call moves to a worker (A9), so queueing and submitting draw on the same allowance rather than two.
post.summary: Queue an assessment scoring and return a job handle

get.description:
`{kind}` selects the response shape, as it does on the submit route: `result` is that instrument's own result model and nothing else, and it is present only once `status` is `succeeded`. There is no shared result envelope here for the same reason there is none there (A12).

`wpll` needs no JWT, because the instrument does not: it is the anonymous teaser, its job has no owner, and the handle is what authorises the poll. The other two scope the handle to the authenticated user.
get.summary: Report the state of a queued assessment scoring

post.description:
Serves the two rules-scored instruments, `core` and `focus_type`, which score deterministically in-process and stay synchronous by design (A19). `{kind}` selects both the request body and the response body -- the route is shared, the payloads are not.

The three provider-scored kinds -- `work_pulse`, `wpll`, `manager_match` -- answer `410 Gone` here since Phase 3c: their scoring moved off the request path, and the problem document's `replaced_by` names the `POST /assessments/{kind}/scoring-jobs` operation that took it.
post.summary: Submit a completed assessment

post.description:
POST /auth/email/verify - Verify the 6-digit OTP sent at registration.

Checks that the code matches, has not expired (default 15 min window), and
clears the token fields on success so the code cannot be reused.
post.summary: Verify the 6-digit code sent at registration

post.description:
POST /auth/email/verify/resend - Issue a fresh OTP for unconfirmed accounts.

Regenerates and re-sends the 6-digit verification code. Rate-limited to 5
per minute to prevent abuse.
post.summary: Issue a fresh verification code for an unconfirmed account

post.description:
POST /auth/login - Authenticate a user and issue a JWT cookie.

Validates credentials, enforces account lockout after MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS
consecutive failures, and requires email confirmation before granting
access. On success, sets an HttpOnly JWT cookie and returns the CSRF token
in the response body (so the frontend can attach it as X-CSRF-TOKEN on
mutating requests).
post.summary: Authenticate a user and issue a JWT cookie

post.description:
POST /auth/logout - Clear the JWT cookie server-side.

Flask-JWT-Extended's unset_jwt_cookies removes the access-token cookie from
the response, effectively ending the session. The JWT itself stays valid
until it expires -- clearing the cookie ends the browser session but cannot
revoke the token, which is what Part 5.3's database-backed refresh tokens
are for.
post.summary: Clear the JWT cookie

post.description: POST /auth/password/forgot - Send a 6-digit OTP for passwordless login.
post.summary: Send a sign-in code to a confirmed account

post.description:
POST /auth/password/reset - Validate OTP and issue a JWT.

Validates the 6-digit OTP, clears it on success, and issues a JWT cookie
plus CSRF token so the user is fully logged in without a password.
post.summary: Exchange a sign-in code for a session

post.description:
POST /auth/register - Create a new user account.

Creates the user with ``email_confirmed=False`` and sends a 6-digit OTP. The
user must confirm their email before they can log in. Profile data is
pre-seeded with a blank default profile appropriate for the given role.

The OTP is written to the outbox inside the same transaction as the account
(Phase 3), so there is no longer a second call here to make it best-effort:
a created account and an owed verification email are one commit.
post.summary: Create an account and send its verification code

get.description:
GET /auth/session - identity, CSRF token, and flags. Writes nothing.

This is the fix for P0-3. The frontend restored its session by calling
GET /profile, which returned the entire profile_data blob and committed an
AuditLog row on the way out -- a write on the hottest read in the system, on
every page load, for data the app shell does not render.

This answers the same question with four identity fields, the CSRF token,
and four booleans, and it does not write. A client that needs the profile
asks GET /me/profile, which is what splitting the god-endpoint bought.
get.summary: Probe the current session without loading the user document

get.description:
GET /companies - one page of companies.

New in Phase 1b: there was no list endpoint, so a screen wanting several
companies fetched the full research document for each one by id.

Paginated with an opaque keyset cursor, never an offset (A5). Pass
next_cursor back as ?cursor= and stop when it comes back null. A cursor the
server did not mint is a 422, not a silent page one -- answering a garbled
cursor with the first page is how a paging loop becomes an infinite one.

parameters.description: Opaque token from a previous next_cursor. Pass back unmodified.
parameters.name: cursor

get.description: GET /companies/<company_id> - Return a company's full profile.
get.summary: Fetch a company's full research profile

post.description:
Replaces `/intake/create-account`, `/intake/sign-in`, `/intake/link-account`, and `/intake/save-to-account`. All four answer the same question -- *this browser holds something anonymous, attach it to an account* -- and differ in which account and where the anonymous thing came from. `mode` is the discriminator and selects the request body, the response body, whether a JWT is required, and which rate-limit bucket the call lands in.

`register` and `sign_in` are public: they are how a visitor *gets* a session, so requiring one would be circular. `link` and `session` require a JWT and the CSRF header with it.

This is `/intake/claims`, not Part 5.2's `/intake/submissions/{id}/claim`, because two of the four modes have no submission id -- `link` files a new submission rather than claiming an existing one, and `session` adopts a quiz session that was never a submission at all.
post.summary: Attach an anonymous submission or quiz session to an account

post.description:
POST /intake/early-access - early-access interest form (no resume).

Writes the lead to the transactional outbox and returns 200; a worker
delivers it to info@solverah.com. This answered 500 on a mail failure until
Phase 3, because the lead existed only as an email and a swallowed error lost
it. The row is durable before this returns, so there is nothing left to lose
and nothing left to report.
post.summary: Register interest from the landing-page modal

post.description:
The unauthenticated half of the quiz-insights pair. Nothing is persisted, because there is no account yet.

Rate-limited per IP *and* under a global daily ceiling. The endpoint this replaces carried `1 per day` keyed on the IP alone, which behind corporate NAT or mobile CGNAT meant one preview per office per day and read to the user as a broken quiz rather than as a limit. See `solverah/api/v1/intelligence.py` for the full reasoning.
post.summary: Generate AI career insights for an unauthenticated preview

post.description: Part 5.2 places this at `/intake/submissions/{id}/resume-ticket`, and it is here instead because the id does not exist yet when this is called. The ticket is what mints it: the flow is ticket -> browser uploads to R2 -> `POST /intake/submissions` commits the row, and no row exists until the last step. A path that takes the id would need either a draft row inserted before any validation ran, or a client-generated id -- and the id is the *only* thing protecting an anonymous submission, so it has to come from a server-side CSPRNG.
post.summary: Request an upload ticket for an anonymous resume submission

post.description:
POST /intake/submissions - commit a submission after the resume upload.

Step 2 of 2. Validates every field, HEADs the uploaded object to confirm it
exists and matches the declared size and type, inserts the row, and sends an
internal notification.

The HEAD is not decoration. The ticket signs a ContentLength, so R2 rejects a
body of a different size -- but nothing stops a client skipping the upload
entirely and calling this anyway. The check is what makes the row mean "a
resume of this size and type exists at this key".
post.summary: Commit an intake submission after the resume upload

delete.description:
DELETE /me - erase personal data; keep de-identified research rows.

Body (JSON): {"confirm": "DELETE"} - an explicit confirmation string, so a
stray click or a replayed request cannot destroy an account.

A body on DELETE is unusual and is the right place for this. It is not a
secret, so a query parameter would work, but a confirmation that travels in
the URL ends up in access logs, proxy caches, and browser history -- and an
intermediary that strips the body fails this closed, with a 400, rather than
open.
delete.summary: Erase personal data, retaining de-identified assessment rows

get.description:
GET /me - identity only: id, email, name, role, confirmation state.

No profileData and no audit row. The client that needs the profile asks
GET /me/profile for it; that is what splitting the god-endpoint bought.

patch.description:
PATCH /me - change the display name.

Name is the only writable identity field. Email is not, because changing it
without re-verification is an account-takeover primitive; role is not,
because an account granting itself a role is a privilege escalation.

get.description: `{kind}` selects the response shape, as on the submit route. Only `work_pulse`, `focus_type`, and `manager_match` store a re-readable result. `core` is absent by design rather than pending -- its scores are withheld from the submit response for a documented reason, and a read endpoint would be the same disclosure through another door.

patch.description:
PATCH /me/career-status - set career_status directly.

A targeted request rather than a full profile save, so the onboarding modal
can record a status without the user filling in experience entries.

get.description:
GET /me/dashboard - profile completion, match count, application count.

recentActivity and recommendations are static placeholders until those
features exist; the three counts are live.
get.summary: Summary statistics for the job-seeker dashboard

get.description: GET /me/export - one JSON document of everything we hold.
get.summary: Export every identified data class held for the authenticated user

get.description:
Replaces `GET /company-lens/matches`, which returned two fixed-size slices -- `best_fits` and `worst_fits` -- in one body, with nothing reachable beyond them. `?order=worst` carries the second slice over: the two halves are now two directions through one paginated list.

Still an O(all-companies) in-process scan that can commit a backfill on the read path (P0-2). The cursor is what lets Phase 2 fix that behind an unchanged contract; it is not itself the fix.

parameters.description: "best" (default) ranks strongest fit first; "worst" ranks weakest first. The endpoint this replaces returned both halves in one body, which is why the parameter exists rather than the client paging to the end.
parameters.name: order

get.summary: Rank companies by fit for the authenticated user

get.description:
GET /me/path-preferences - the three saved preferences, or nulls.

New in Phase 1b: the endpoint this pairs with was write-only, so a client
wanting to show the user their own answers had to keep a copy or read them
out of the profile blob.
get.summary: Read the user's career search preferences

put.description:
PUT /me/path-preferences - write all three preferences.

PUT rather than the POST this replaces, because the write replaces the whole
set rather than merging into it. Returns the saved document instead of
`{"message": "Preferences saved"}`, so a client does not have to make a
second call to see what it stored.

Each value is checked against a closed set: the path scorer branches on all
three, so an unrecognised one would silently change ranking rather than fail.
put.summary: Replace the user's career search preferences

post.description:
The only way path suggestions are computed since Phase 3c. Queues the O*NET and OpenAI fan-out and answers `202` with a job handle; poll `GET /me/path-suggestion-jobs/{job_id}` until `status` is `succeeded` or `failed`.

A succeeded job warms the per-user cache `GET /me/path-suggestions` serves, so the payload can be re-read there without paying for the scoring twice.

Rate limited, and the cache-reading `GET` is not: an enqueue returns immediately and can be issued in a loop, so the budget that bounds provider spend has to live here (A9).
post.summary: Queue a path-suggestion scoring and return a job handle

get.description:
GET /me/path-suggestion-jobs/{job_id} - poll a queued scoring.

404 covers no such job, a malformed handle, and somebody else's job alike.
Distinguishing them would confirm that a handle exists, which is the only
thing protecting one.

`error` on a failed job carries the scorer's own message -- notably
`career_status_not_set`, the same condition the synchronous GET answers 400
for, which the client handles by prompting for the missing field rather than
by retrying.
get.summary: Report the state of a queued path-suggestion scoring

get.description:
Serves the per-user cache that a succeeded path-suggestion job populates; the cache is invalidated when Work Pulse results, experience entries, or ManagerMatch results change.

A miss is `404` and computes nothing: the problem document's `start_job_url` names `POST /me/path-suggestion-jobs`, which queues the O*NET and OpenAI fan-out this route performed inline before Phase 3c and whose poll returns the same payload this serves.
get.summary: Read the cached career path suggestions

get.description:
GET /me/profile - the profile blob, in an envelope.

Records a `read` audit event. Unlike the endpoint this replaces, that write
is no longer on the session-restore path, which is what made it P0-3.
get.summary: Read the authenticated user's profile document

patch.description:
PATCH /me/profile - merge incoming keys into the stored profile.

Unknown keys are stripped by clean_profile_data rather than rejected. Quiz
results merge at the sub-key level so existing entries survive. Edits are
diffed against the stored parser snapshot to record ResumeParseCorrection
rows for anything the user changed after a resume upload.

Still a read-modify-write of a whole JSON column (P0-1), and still without a
version to check. Phase 2 is what fixes that; the envelope this returns is
where the version will go.
patch.summary: Merge a partial profile over the stored document

post.description:
POST /me/quiz-insights - generate and persist AI career insights.

Validates and normalizes the quiz answers, calls OpenAI with a structured
prompt, coerces the response to a canonical schema, and persists the result
into profile_data.quizInsights.
post.summary: Generate and persist AI career insights

get.description:
GET /me/recommendations - a page of job recommendations.

Always empty today: the ML pipeline that produced these was replaced by the
AI agent and the Groq-backed replacement is not wired up.

Paginated anyway, and that is deliberate. The envelope is the contract, so
the day this starts returning rows is not the day every client changes.

post.description:
POST /me/recommendations/refresh - trigger recommendation generation.

A no-op stub while the Groq-based flow is being built. Part 5.2 has this
answering 202 with a job handle; that arrives with Phase 3's queue, at which
point there is real work for the handle to refer to.
post.summary: Trigger job recommendation generation

get.description:
GET /me/resume-parse-jobs/{job_id} - poll a queued parse.

404 covers three cases deliberately: no such job, a malformed handle, and a
job belonging to somebody else. Distinguishing them would confirm that a
handle exists, which is the only thing protecting one.
get.summary: Report the state of a queued resume parse

post.description:
POST /me/resumes - presign a PUT URL for a resume upload. Step 1 of 2.

Returns a resume_id rather than the raw object key the superseded endpoint
handed back. The key is derived server-side from the JWT identity, so a
caller has no key to name and the finalize step has no prefix check to get
wrong.
post.summary: Request an upload ticket for a new resume

get.description:
GET /me/resumes/{resume_id}/download-url - short-lived presigned GET URL.

`current` is a valid resume_id and means "the resume on my profile". The
blob holds exactly one resumeKey, so until Phase 2 gives resumes their own
rows that is the only one a client can name without having just uploaded it.
get.summary: Presign a download URL for a stored resume

post.description: Step 2 of 2 of a resume upload, and the only step 2 since Phase 3c deleted the synchronous `POST /me/resumes/{resume_id}/complete`. Answers `202` with a job handle instead of blocking for the parse. Poll `GET /me/resume-parse-jobs/{job_id}` until `status` is `succeeded` or `failed`.
post.summary: Queue a resume parse and return a job handle

get.description:
GET /me/skills - proficiency ratings and whether they are confirmed.

New in Phase 1b. The superseded endpoint was write-only, so the client had
to read the whole profile document to find out what it had already saved.

put.description:
PUT /me/skills - write the full set of proficiency ratings.

PUT rather than the PATCH this replaces, because the write is a wholesale
replacement of the ratings map, not a merge into it. Also sets
skills_proficiency_confirmed so the rating modal stops re-prompting.
